g9-economics-ue5-t1.overview: Production is the process of combining inputs such as labour, land and capital to create outputs that satisfy human wants. This lesson defines production, sorts inputs into fixed and variable types, and separates tangible from intangible outputs.
objectives: Define production and explain how inputs are converted into outputs
Identify the four basic inputs used in the production of goods and services
Distinguish between tangible and intangible outputs with examples
Differentiate fixed inputs from variable inputs
Apply input-output analysis to a real production activity in Ethiopia
g9-economics-ue5-t1.simple: Production is the act of combining inputs to create an output, either a good or a service, that adds utility for people. Growing wheat on a plot of land using labour, capital and seeds is production. Inputs are the economic resources used in production: labour, capital, land and entrepreneurial ability. Outputs are the results of the production process, and they can be tangible or intangible. Tangible outputs are physical things you can see and touch, like machinery or a car. Intangible outputs are services with value but no physical form, like insurance, software or health care. Inputs are also divided into fixed inputs, whose quantity cannot be changed during the period, such as buildings and machinery, and variable inputs, which can be changed, such as raw materials and labour.
g9-economics-ue5-t1.detailed:
What production is. Production is a process of combining various inputs to produce an output for consumption. It is the act of creating output in the form of a commodity or a service which contributes to the utility of individuals. In other words, production converts inputs into outputs. For example, when we produce wheat on a plot of land with the help of inputs like labour, capital and seeds, it is termed as production of wheat. A service such as a doctor's consultation, a bank transaction or a bus ride is also production, because it creates utility.

The inputs. Inputs are economic resources that can be used in the production of goods and services. In economics there are four basic inputs commonly used in production: labour (human effort), capital (machines, tools and buildings), land (natural resources and plots), and entrepreneurial ability (the skill of organizing the other inputs and taking risk). The entrepreneur combines the other three factors to bring output to the market.

The outputs. Outputs are inputs transformed into final usable form, because inputs by themselves give less satisfaction to the consumer. Outputs are the consequences of the production process. A mill transforms wheat into flour; a garment factory transforms cotton and skill into shirts; a school transforms teaching into trained students.

Tangible and intangible outputs. Outputs are classified into tangible and intangible ones. Tangible outputs are physical products that can be touched; they have a physical existence, such as buildings, machinery, equipment and cars, which have long term physical existence. Intangible outputs may have value but are not physical objects; a person cannot see or touch them. Examples include insurance coverage, consultancy service, computer software, educational training and health care service. These cannot often be tried out, inspected or tested in advance. The main difference is physical existence: tangible output can be seen or touched, while intangible output cannot.

Fixed and variable inputs. Inputs are divided into two main groups by whether their quantity can be changed during the period under consideration. A fixed input is one whose quantity cannot be varied during the period; building and machinery are examples. A variable input is one whose quantity can be changed during the period; raw materials and labour are examples. This distinction is the foundation of the short run and long run analysis you will meet in the next lesson.

Why the classification matters. Knowing which inputs are fixed and which are variable tells a producer how output can be increased right now. If a farmer cannot buy another ox plough this season, he can still raise output by hiring more labour and applying more seed and fertilizer, the variable inputs. Later, in the long run, he can change the fixed inputs too, by buying more land or machinery. Sound production decisions always start from this input-output picture.

workedExamples.problem: A farmer in Gojjam grows wheat on one hectare of land, using family labour, an ox plough, seed and fertilizer. Identify the inputs and the output of this production process.
workedExamples.given: Land (one hectare), family labour, ox plough (capital), seed and fertilizer; the product is wheat.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: production combines inputs - land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship - to obtain an output.
workedExamples.substitution: Land, labour, ox plough, seed and fertilizer are the inputs; wheat is the output.
workedExamples.calculation: The farmer transforms these inputs through the growing season into a wheat harvest that consumers can use.
workedExamples.answer: Inputs: land, labour, capital (ox plough) and materials like seed; output: wheat, a tangible output.

workedExamples.problem: Classify each item as a tangible or intangible output: computer software, a delivery truck, health care service, machinery, insurance coverage, a school building.
workedExamples.given: Six produced items, some physical and some not.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: tangible outputs have physical existence and can be touched; intangible outputs have value but cannot be seen or touched.
workedExamples.substitution: Software, health care and insurance are not physical objects; the truck, machinery and building are.
workedExamples.calculation: Tangible: truck, machinery, school building. Intangible: software, health care service, insurance coverage.
workedExamples.answer: Tangible - truck, machinery, building; intangible - software, health care, insurance.

workedExamples.problem: A bakery wants to increase output this month. Its resources are the oven and building, flour, sugar, electricity and hourly-paid workers. Which inputs are fixed and which are variable?
workedExamples.given: Oven and building cannot be enlarged this month; flour, sugar, electricity and worker hours can be adjusted at any time.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a fixed input cannot be varied during the period; a variable input can.
workedExamples.substitution: The oven and building are fixed inputs; flour, sugar, electricity and labour are variable inputs.
workedExamples.calculation: The bakery can only raise output by using more of the variable inputs together with the fixed oven and building.
workedExamples.answer: Fixed inputs - oven and building; variable inputs - flour, sugar, electricity and labour.

workedExamples.problem: List the inputs used in the teaching-learning process of your classroom and identify the outputs.
workedExamples.given: Activity 5.1 of the textbook asks students to observe the inputs of teaching and learning.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: inputs are the economic resources used in production; outputs are the results obtained.
workedExamples.substitution: Inputs include the teacher's labour, the classroom, blackboard, textbooks, chalk and electricity; the students' own effort and time.
workedExamples.calculation: The process combines these inputs over the school year to produce educated students.
workedExamples.answer: Input: teacher's labour, classroom and materials; output: an intangible one, education and trained students.

commonMistakes: Thinking production means only making physical goods, forgetting that services like health care and education are also outputs.
Calling raw materials fixed inputs; raw materials and labour are the classic variable inputs.
Assuming buildings and machinery can be changed any time; in a given period they are fixed inputs.
Believing inputs and outputs are the same thing; outputs are inputs transformed into a usable form.
Classifying computer software or insurance as tangible outputs because you can buy them, when they are intangible.
Forgetting entrepreneurial ability as the fourth basic input alongside land, labour and capital.
Thinking only the final consumer good counts as output, ignoring services and intermediate goods.
applications: A wheat farm in Gojjam combines land, labour, seed and an ox plough to harvest a tangible output.
An Ethiopian Airlines flight sells an intangible output: a transport service you cannot touch.
A garment factory in an industrial park turns cotton and labour into shirts for export.
Even if a clinic cannot expand its building this year, it can serve more patients with more staff hours and medicine, its variable inputs.
A coffee exporter identifies the four basic inputs before deciding whether to buy more land or hire more pickers.
Software firms in Addis Ababa produce intangible outputs whose value is real although nothing physical is delivered.
g9-economics-ue5-t1.summary: Production converts inputs into outputs: it combines labour, capital, land and entrepreneurial ability to create goods and services that add utility. Outputs are tangible when they have physical existence, like machinery, and intangible when they do not, like insurance or software. Inputs are fixed when their quantity cannot be changed in the period and variable when it can, a distinction that prepares the short run and long run analysis of the next lesson.

g9-economics-ue5-t2.overview: Production periods are classified not by the calendar but by how flexible the inputs are. This lesson defines short run and long run and shows how total product, average product and marginal product measure the productivity of a variable input in the short run.
objectives: Define the short run and the long run in terms of input flexibility
Explain why short run and long run are not calendar periods
Define total product, average product and marginal product
Compute average product and marginal product from a production table
Identify the stages of short run production using a production schedule
g9-economics-ue5-t2.simple: The periods of production are classified by the flexibility of economic resources. The short run is the period in which at least one input is fixed while the remaining inputs are variable, so a producer can raise output only by using more variable inputs like labour and raw materials. The long run is the period in which all inputs are variable, so a firm can build a new plant or factory and change its size. These are not calendar periods like one year or five years; they describe the economic arrangement of inputs. Productivity in the short run is measured by total product (TP), the overall output; average product (AP = TP/L), output per worker; and marginal product (MP), the extra output from one more unit of input.
g9-economics-ue5-t2.detailed:
How the periods are classified. The classification of periods of production is based on the degree of flexibility of economic resources to changes in the business environment. The two periods are the short run and the long run. Flexibility means which inputs the firm can change when conditions change; it is not about the clock or the calendar.

The short run. The short run is a period of production in which at least one of the inputs is fixed while the remaining inputs are variable. An increase in output in the short run can be brought about only by increasing the variable inputs. For example, if a producer wishes to increase output in the short run, she can use more labour and more raw materials while the factory building and machines stay as they are.

The long run. The long run is a period of production in which all inputs are variable and there is no fixed input. A firm can install a new plant or construct a new factory building; the long run is the period during which the size of the plant can be changed. Thus all factors of production are variable in the long run.

Not a calendar measure. When we say short run and long run we do not necessarily mean a short or long period of time like one year, less than one year, two or five years. We refer to the nature of the economic arrangement of the inputs in response to the changing economic environment. A small fruit juice seller may be in the long run after a week, because she can rent a bigger kiosk quickly; a cement factory may remain in the short run for years, because its plant cannot be changed quickly.

Measuring productivity: total product. Total product (TP) is the overall amount of output produced by the factors of production employed over a given period; it is the gross or entire output by workers, expressed as Quantity (Q). In the short run, the firm obtains its total product by combining variable inputs with a specific amount of fixed inputs.

Average product and marginal product. Average product (AP) is obtained by dividing the total output by the number of workers employed: AP = TP/L, where TP is total product and L is labour. Average product is a good indicator of the productivity of labour, and productivity is a measure of output per unit of input. Marginal product (MP) is, holding other factors constant, the increase in output which results from using one additional unit of a single factor input; MP = change in TP divided by change in L. Both MP and AP of labour are derived from TP, so the three measures are interrelated.

Stages of short run production. Table 5.1 of the textbook shows a production function with one variable input (labour) and one fixed input (capital, 10 units). Product rises from 0 to 108 quintals as workers increase from 0 to 7, then falls when the 8th worker is added. The textbook marks Stage I (0 to 4 workers, where AP rises from 10 to 19), Stage II (5 to 7 workers, where MP falls from 19 to 13 and then reaches 0 when TP is at its maximum of 108), and Stage III (8 workers and beyond, where MP is negative and total product actually falls from 108 to 96 to 80). Reading a production schedule this way tells a firm how many variable-input units are worth employing.

keyTerms.def: A period of production in which at least one input is fixed and the others are variable, so output rises only through the variable inputs.
A period of production in which all inputs are variable and the size of the plant can be changed.
The overall amount of output produced by the factors employed over a given period; the entire output expressed in Quantity (Q).
Total output divided by the number of workers employed, AP = TP/L; a good indicator of the productivity of labour.
The increase in output resulting from using one additional unit of a variable input while other factors are held constant; MP = change in TP / change in L.
A measure of output per unit of input, the output ratio for each level of input and the corresponding level of output.
The three ranges of the short run production function: Stage I (rising AP), Stage II (MP falling to zero) and Stage III (MP negative).
An input whose quantity cannot be varied within the period under consideration, such as capital in the short run.

workedExamples.problem: Using Table 5.1, find the average product and the marginal product of the 3rd worker.
workedExamples.given: Table 5.1: with 2 workers TP = 28 quintals; with 3 workers TP = 51 quintals (capital fixed at 10).
workedExamples.formula: AP = TP/L and MP = change in TP / change in L.
workedExamples.substitution: AP of 3 workers = 51/3; MP of the 3rd worker = (51 - 28)/(3 - 2).
workedExamples.answer: AP = 17 quintals per worker; MP = 23 quintals, exactly as shown in Table 5.1.

workedExamples.problem: What is the marginal product of the 8th worker in Table 5.1, and which stage of production begins there?
workedExamples.given: With 7 workers TP = 108 quintals; with 8 workers TP = 96 quintals.
workedExamples.formula: MP = change in TP / change in L.
workedExamples.calculation: 96 - 108 = -12, so the 8th worker reduces output by 12 quintals.
workedExamples.answer: MP = -12 quintals; the negative marginal product marks the beginning of Stage III, and the textbook also gives AP = 12 there.

workedExamples.problem: At which number of workers is total product at its maximum, and what is the marginal product there?
workedExamples.given: Table 5.1: TP = 108 at both 6 and 7 workers; capital fixed at 10.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: TP is at its maximum where the marginal product reaches zero.
workedExamples.substitution: Adding the 7th worker changes TP from 108 to 108, an increase of 0.
workedExamples.calculation: MP of the 7th worker = (108 - 108)/1 = 0, and TP cannot rise further.
workedExamples.answer: TP is maximum at 108 quintals with 7 workers, where MP = 0 (Stage II ends).

workedExamples.problem: Ato Kebede employs 4 workers on fixed capital of 10 units and harvests 76 quintals; with 5 workers he harvests 95 quintals. Compute the average product with 4 workers and the marginal product of the 5th, and state the stage.
workedExamples.given: TP(4) = 76, TP(5) = 95, L rises from 4 to 5.
workedExamples.formula: AP = TP/L; MP = change in TP / change in L.
workedExamples.calculation: 76/4 = 19; 95 - 76 = 19; AP and MP are equal at 19 at this point.
workedExamples.answer: AP = 19 and MP = 19, the boundary marked Stage II in Table 5.1; AP has just stopped rising.

commonMistakes: Thinking the short run always means less than one year and the long run means years; they are defined by input flexibility, not the calendar.
Assuming a firm can increase output by any means in the short run; in the short run only the variable inputs can be increased.
Confusing average product with marginal product; AP is output per worker, MP is the extra output of one more worker.
Computing MP by dividing TP by L; MP is the change in TP between rows, not TP/L.
Forgetting that MP can be negative; adding workers beyond Stage II lowers total product.
Believing the long run has fixed inputs; in the long run every input, including plant size, is variable.
Ignoring the fixed input when reading a production table; Table 5.1 holds capital fixed at 10 units.
applications: A fruit juice shop can hire an extra helper today (short run), but can only rent a bigger kiosk after weeks of planning (long run).
A cement factory in Oromia cannot change its kilns quickly, so extra output must come from more materials and shifts, variable inputs.
A farmer decides how many daily labourers to hire for harvest by watching when the marginal product of an extra worker falls toward zero.
A bank branch with a fixed building raises output in the short run by adding tellers, and expands its premises only in the long run.
Ethiopian Airlines adds flights (variable) with its current fleet in the short run, but buys new aircraft to raise capacity in the long run.
The government's coffee extension officer uses average product per worker to compare productivity between two woredas.
g9-economics-ue5-t2.summary: Production periods are classified by input flexibility, not by time: the short run keeps at least one input fixed so output rises only through variable inputs, while the long run makes all inputs variable and even the plant size changeable. Short run productivity is measured by total product, average product (AP = TP/L) and marginal product (MP = change in TP over change in L). Table 5.1 shows three stages: AP rises in Stage I, MP falls to zero at maximum TP in Stage II, and MP turns negative in Stage III.

g9-economics-ue5-t3.overview: Cost of production is the total expenditure and sacrifice made in producing and distributing goods and services. This lesson separates explicit from implicit costs, economic from accounting cost, fixed from variable cost, and builds total, average and marginal cost from Table 5.2.
objectives: Define the cost of production and relate it to the production process
Distinguish explicit costs from implicit costs with examples
Differentiate economic cost from accounting cost
Explain fixed costs and variable costs and how total cost is formed
Calculate total, average and marginal cost from a short run cost table
g9-economics-ue5-t3.simple: Cost of production refers to the monetary outlays, expenditures and sacrifices made in the entire process of production and distribution. Explicit costs are actual cash payments to outsiders, such as wages, rent, raw materials, fuel and power; accountants record them, so they are called accounting costs. Implicit costs are the values of self-owned, non-purchased resources, like the owner's unpaid work or the rent a firm could have earned from its own building, valued at their best alternative use. Economic cost equals implicit plus explicit costs, while accounting cost counts only purchased inputs. Fixed costs do not vary with output, such as rent and interest; variable costs do, such as wages of workers and raw materials. Total cost is TC = TFC + TVC.
g9-economics-ue5-t3.detailed:
Cost and production are inseparable. The cost of production generally refers to the monetary outlays associated with production activity, or the total expenditures and sacrifices made in the entire process of production and distribution of goods and services. Every input the firm employs must be paid or sacrificed, so studying production leads directly to studying cost.

Explicit costs. Explicit costs are the actual monetary payments or cash outlays that firms make to outsiders who supply inputs or resources. The rewards of labour, land, capital and entrepreneurs are all costs for a firm that employs them; payments for raw materials, fuel, transport and power are also costs. Such usually-out-of-pocket costs are termed accounting costs, because accounting cost refers to the cost of purchased inputs only, and this only refers to the explicit cost.

Implicit costs. Implicit costs stand for the values of non-purchased resources owned and used by firms in their own production activities. Examples are the salary of an owner-manager who takes no wage, or the estimated rent of a building that belongs to the owner of the firm. The values of these self-owned resources should be estimated from what they could earn in their best alternative uses - that is, by opportunity cost.

Economic cost versus accounting cost. Economists and accountants define and treat costs differently. Economists define costs in terms of opportunity costs and include implicit costs in profit calculations: Economic cost = Implicit costs + Explicit costs. Accounting cost, by contrast, is the monetary value of all purchased inputs used in production; it ignores non-purchased, self-owned inputs and considers only direct expenses such as wages and salaries, raw materials, depreciation allowances, interest on borrowed funds and utility expenses like electricity, water and telephone.

Fixed and variable costs. Fixed costs do not vary as the firm changes its level of output; they are always incurred even if the firm produces nothing, and they are the costs of fixed inputs. Examples are rents on leased properties, interest on borrowed funds, the wear and tear of machinery, and the cost of administrative staff. Variable costs directly vary with the level of output: when output is zero, variable costs are zero, and as the firm expands output these costs rise. Examples include the wages of workers other than administrative staff and the cost of raw materials.

Total cost and Table 5.2. Total cost is the sum of total fixed cost and total variable cost: TC = TFC + TVC. Table 5.2 of the textbook shows a short run cost table: TFC is birr 60 even when output is zero, so the TFC line is parallel to the quantity axis at 60 birr above it. TVC is zero when output is zero, and rises as output rises - initially at a decreasing rate, but later at an increasing rate, because at first few variable inputs are combined with the fixed inputs and later more and more variable inputs squeeze against them. Since TC is the sum of TVC and TFC at every output level, the TC curve has the same shape as TVC. In the table: Q = 0 gives TFC 60, TVC 0, TC 60; Q = 1 gives 60 + 20 = 80; Q = 2 gives 100; Q = 3 gives 120; Q = 4 gives 125; Q = 5 gives 135; and Q = 6 gives 60 + 120 = 180 birr.

Average and marginal cost. Average total cost (ATC) is the total cost per unit of output: ATC = TC/Q. It splits into average fixed cost AFC = TFC/Q and average variable cost AVC = TVC/Q, so that AFC + AVC = ATC. Marginal cost (MC) is the extra or additional total cost that results from producing one more unit of output: MC = change in TC divided by change in Q. Since total fixed cost does not change in the short run, MC = change in TVC divided by change in Q.

keyTerms.def: The monetary outlays, total expenditures and sacrifices made in the entire process of production and distribution of goods and services.
Actual monetary payments or cash outlays made to outsiders who supply inputs, such as wages, rent, raw materials, fuel and power.
The value of non-purchased, self-owned resources used by the firm, estimated from their best alternative use, such as an owner's unpaid work.
The monetary value of all purchased inputs used in production; it ignores self-owned inputs and counts only explicit costs.
Implicit costs plus explicit costs; the opportunity-cost view of the economist.
Costs that do not vary with the level of output, incurred even when output is zero, such as rent and interest.
Costs that directly vary with the level of output; zero when output is zero, rising as output expands, such as raw materials.
The additional total cost of producing one more unit of output; in the short run it equals the change in total variable cost.

workedExamples.problem: Using Table 5.2 of the textbook, confirm the total cost when the firm produces 5 units of output.
workedExamples.given: At Q = 5: TFC = 60 birr (which stays 60 at every output, even zero) and TVC = 75 birr.
workedExamples.answer: TC = 135 birr, exactly the value shown in Table 5.2 for Q = 5.

workedExamples.problem: From Table 5.2, compute the average total cost, average fixed cost and average variable cost when output is 4.
workedExamples.given: At Q = 4: TFC = 60 birr, TVC = 65 birr, so TC = 125 birr.
workedExamples.formula: ATC = TC/Q, with AFC = TFC/Q and AVC = TVC/Q, and AFC + AVC = ATC.
workedExamples.answer: ATC = 31.25 birr per unit, made up of AFC = 15 birr and AVC = 16.25 birr.

workedExamples.problem: Using Table 5.2, find the marginal cost of raising output from 5 units to 6 units.
workedExamples.given: TC at Q = 5 is 135 birr; TC at Q = 6 is 180 birr (TFC 60 plus TVC 120).
workedExamples.formula: MC = change in TC / change in Q; in the short run MC = change in TVC / change in Q.
workedExamples.answer: MC = 45 birr for the 6th unit; the jump is large because TVC rose at an increasing rate here.

workedExamples.problem: A firm in Bahir Dar records explicit costs of 100,000 birr per month. The owner works without a salary though she could earn 30,000 birr elsewhere, and the firm occupies its own building which could rent for 10,000 birr. Find the economic cost and compare it with the accounting cost.
workedExamples.given: Explicit costs = 100,000 birr; forgone salary = 30,000 birr; forgone rent = 10,000 birr.
workedExamples.formula: Economic cost = Implicit costs + Explicit costs; Accounting cost = Explicit costs only.
workedExamples.calculation: 100,000 + 40,000 = 140,000 birr economic cost, versus 100,000 birr accounting cost.
workedExamples.answer: Economic cost = 140,000 birr, which is 40,000 birr higher than the accounting cost of 100,000 birr.

commonMistakes: Believing fixed cost exists only when the firm produces; TFC is incurred even at zero output, as Table 5.2 shows with 60 birr.
Treating the owner's unpaid salary or the rent of an own building as free; these are implicit costs that economists include.
Thinking economic cost and accounting cost are identical; economic cost adds implicit costs to explicit ones.
Calling the wages of all workers fixed cost; wages of ordinary workers vary with output, while administrative staff costs are fixed.
Computing marginal cost as TC/Q; that is average total cost, while MC is the change in TC per extra unit.
Forgetting that AFC + AVC = ATC when splitting average cost.
Assuming variable cost rises at a constant rate; TVC first rises at a decreasing rate, then at an increasing rate.
applications: A wheat flour factory pays rent and loan interest (fixed costs) whether it mills or not, but flour inputs and shift wages vary with output (variable costs).
A family shop in Hawassa must count the owner's own unpaid hours as implicit cost to judge real profit.
A new graduate comparing a job offer with opening a shop should add forgone salary to the true economic cost of the business.
A textile firm computes ATC per shirt from its cost table to decide a competitive export price.
A maize trader raising purchases from 5 to 6 trucks checks the marginal cost of the extra truck before committing.
School clubs budgeting for a science fair separate fixed costs, like a rented tent, from variable costs, like materials per stall.
g9-economics-ue5-t3.summary: Cost of production is the total monetary outlay and sacrifice of producing and distributing goods. Explicit costs are cash payments to outsiders and form the accounting cost, while implicit costs value self-owned resources at their best alternative use, so economic cost = implicit + explicit costs. Fixed costs like rent and interest do not vary with output, variable costs like raw materials and wages do, and TC = TFC + TVC, from which ATC = TC/Q (with AFC + AVC = ATC) and MC = change in TC per unit are derived, as Table 5.2 illustrates with TFC fixed at 60 birr.

items: Interest, wear and tear, admin staff

pairs.q: Why are explicit costs called accounting costs?
pairs.a: Because they are out-of-pocket costs for purchased inputs, which accountants record.
Economic cost = Implicit costs + Explicit costs.

pairs.q: What is TFC at zero output in Table 5.2?
pairs.a: 60 birr; fixed cost is incurred even when nothing is produced.

pairs.q: What does marginal cost equal in the short run?
pairs.a: The change in total variable cost per extra unit, since TFC does not change.

questions.q: The cost of production refers to:
options: only the wages paid to workers
the total expenditures and sacrifices in production and distribution
only the price of raw materials
questions.explanation: Cost of production covers all monetary outlays and sacrifices in the entire process of production and distribution.

questions.q: Which of the following is an implicit cost?
options: The estimated rent of a building owned by the firm
questions.explanation: Implicit costs are the values of self-owned resources, like forgone rent on an own building.

questions.q: Accounting cost includes implicit costs.
questions.explanation: Accounting cost counts only purchased inputs, the explicit costs; economists add implicit costs to get economic cost.

questions.q: Write the identity relating economic cost to implicit and explicit costs.
questions.explanation: Economic cost = Implicit costs + Explicit costs, as defined by economists.

questions.q: Using TC = TFC + TVC, the total cost at Q = 3 in Table 5.2 is:
questions.explanation: TFC = 60 and TVC = 60 at Q = 3, so TC = 120 birr.

questions.q: Compute the average total cost when Q = 2 from Table 5.2, where TFC = 60 and TVC = 40.
questions.explanation: TC = 100, so ATC = TC/Q = 100/2 = 50 birr per unit.

questions.q: When output is zero, variable costs are also zero.
questions.explanation: Variable costs depend on the level of output and are zero at zero output.

questions.q: In Table 5.2, TVC rises at a decreasing rate at first and then at an increasing rate because:
options: the firm first combines few variable inputs with the fixed ones, then more and more
questions.explanation: The textbook explains the TVC shape by how variable inputs combine with the fixed inputs over time.

questions.q: Explain why marginal cost can be calculated as the change in TVC instead of the change in TC in the short run.
questions.answer: TFC does not change|fixed cost is constant
questions.explanation: Since total fixed cost never changes in the short run, the whole change in TC comes from TVC.

questions.q: Give the abbreviation identity that links total cost, total fixed cost and total variable cost.
questions.explanation: Total cost equals total fixed cost plus total variable cost.

questions.q: A firm's marginal cost of the 6th unit in Table 5.2 is 45 birr because:
questions.explanation: MC = change in TC = 180 - 135 = 45 birr between Q = 5 and Q = 6.
